evidence.limitations: Not independently re-verified against the primary table in this session; taken as given and used only for angular-to-physical scale conversion.
N-body/dynamical-model mass, not directly used by the light-emissivity profile in this recipe; recorded for completeness and for the mass-segregation limitation below.

This is a 3D mass radius from a dynamical model, not a directly observed projected quantity. Used here (via an approximate projected/3D scaling, see projected-half-light-approx) to fix the King concentration of a separately assumed *light* profile; mass and light radii can differ under mass segregation.
Used as an approximation for the projected King core radius (approximation A in king-abel-profile.json); no independent photometric King fit for this specific radius was located in this session.
Recorded for completeness; not used to scale the recipe's relative emissivity, which is unitless display light, not calibrated luminosity.
Kinematic evidence, not used in this image/light recipe; recorded because it is part of the measured structural package and could support a future kinematic cross-check.

evidence.scope: Whole cluster; varies with radius across the literature (roughly 0.08 core to ~0.19 outskirts)
evidence.limitations: This is the primary evidence AGAINST the sphericity assumption used everywhere else in this ledger. Omega Centauri is a measurably flattened, rotating cluster; every quantity below that assumes spherical symmetry is only a first-order approximation to its real triaxial/oblate shape.

evidence.quantity: publisher pointing center vs. independent catalogue position
evidence.limitations: This confirms the publisher WCS center matches the independently catalogued cluster center to sub-pixel accuracy (0.24 arcsec vs. 0.21 arcsec/px). It is a whole-field sanity check, not a star-by-star astrometric fit against an external catalogue (e.g. Gaia); no such per-star fit was performed in this session.

value.formula: Sigma(R) proportional to [ (1+(R/rc)^2)^-1/2 - (1+(rt/rc)^2)^-1/2 ]^2 for R <= rt

evidence.scope: Adopted profile family for the projected light distribution
evidence.limitations: Standard single-mass isotropic empirical law; Omega Centauri has multiple stellar populations and measurable rotation/flattening that a single-mass spherical King law does not capture.

evidence.quantity: projected half-light radius as a fraction of the 3D half-mass radius
evidence.scope: Used once, to convert the measured 3D half-mass radius into a target projected half-light radius for solving the King concentration
evidence.limitations: This factor is an approximate, broadly-applicable result for centrally concentrated dispersion-supported systems, not a value measured for Omega Centauri specifically.

evidence.quantity: spherically symmetric 3D relative emissivity vs. radius, derived by Abel-inverting the fitted King projected profile
evidence.scope: 0 to the solved tidal radius (46.4 pc)
evidence.limitations: Deterministic consequence of assumed spherical symmetry plus the King profile family and its two fixed shape parameters (approximations A and B recorded in king-abel-profile.json). It is not a released, independently measured 3D point table; it is our own Abel-inversion computation from measured/published-model inputs. The single strongest physical limitation is sphericity itself: Omega Centauri's true ellipticity (~0.08-0.19, entry 'ellipticity') means the real 3D structure is oblate/triaxial, not spherical, and this profile cannot represent that flattening.

evidence.quantity: status note, not a physical quantity
evidence.limitations: The lab's only currently implemented method that treats an external prior as 'broad shape from the prior, detail fitted from the image' (simulation-guided-finite-emission@1 / two-scale) requires a pre-existing fixed-density Alignment reconstruction (a 'baselineId') built from an N-body particle simulation via prepare-full-density. No such simulation or baseline exists for a globular cluster, and building one would mean writing new object-preparation tooling, which this task explicitly excludes. See README.md.

evidence.quantity: inclination of the cluster's symmetry axis to the line of sight
evidence.scope: Whole cluster; axisymmetric Schwarzschild orbit-superposition model fit to line-of-sight velocities plus internal proper motions
evidence.limitations: This is a dynamical-model result, not a direct geometric measurement: it assumes the cluster is exactly axisymmetric (oblate, one symmetry axis) and infers inclination from how well that assumed shape reproduces the observed kinematics. The same paper reports a dynamical distance of 4.8 +/- 0.3 kpc, which is in tension with the 5430 +/- 50 pc value used elsewhere in this ledger (Baumgardt & Vasiliev 2021); the two papers used independent methods and do not agree to within their stated errors, which is itself evidence that the axisymmetric model is not a perfect fit.

evidence.scope: Inner few arcminutes, from combined HST+MUSE proper motions (plane-of-sky rotation)
evidence.limitations: Differs from van de Ven et al. (2006)'s i = 50 +/- 4 deg by about 1.5-2 sigma using much better proper-motion data restricted to the inner region. Both cannot be simultaneously exactly right; this disagreement is direct evidence that the inclination of a single rigid oblate model is not fully converged in the published literature, only bracketed to roughly 40-55 degrees.

Directly observed rotation signal (not a model output), but only along the line of sight; does not by itself give a 3D rotation axis or amplitude. Velocity dispersion drops from about 15 km/s in the inner few arcmin to about 6 km/s at 25 arcmin, so the rotation amplitude is a sizeable fraction of the local dispersion in the outer cluster.

evidence.scope: Earlier radial-velocity dataset, independent of Reijns et al. (2006)
evidence.limitations: Recorded from a search-engine summary of the paper, not a direct fetch of the paper text in this session, so treat the exact 7.9 km/s figure as approximate pending primary verification. Given alongside rotation-amplitude-reijns-2006 to show two independent studies agree the amplitude is of order 6-8 km/s, not to imply a precise consensus number.

evidence.quantity: whether rotation alone explains the photometric flattening

value.conclusion: not fully; a purely rotationally-flattened oblate isotropic model under-/over-predicts the observed ellipticity profile at some radii, and matching it needs added radial velocity anisotropy

evidence.scope: Whole cluster, axisymmetric rotating-anisotropic dynamical models
evidence.limitations: This is model-dependent evidence, not a raw measurement. Its direct consequence for this ledger: an oblate model built only from a measured ellipticity, position angle and inclination (isotropic King/Wilson made oblate) is known to be an approximation even under the axisymmetric assumption; velocity anisotropy, not just rotation, contributes to the real shape.

evidence.scope: Innermost ~20 arcsec (~0.5 pc), MUSE narrow+wide field integral-field spectroscopy
evidence.limitations: Direct observational evidence that the cluster's inner few tenths of a parsec rotate opposite to the bulk cluster rotation. This is incompatible with a single rigid-body oblate rotation pattern extended all the way to the center; any oblate King/Wilson model built from bulk ellipticity/PA/inclination necessarily misses this innermost feature, which occupies a negligible fraction of the cluster's volume but is a real, measured departure from simple oblate rotation.

A model-inferred substructure (about 4% of total mass) in the same dynamical fit that gives the headline inclination number above; recorded because it is additional evidence that the cluster's true structure is not a single smooth oblate body, even though it is a small mass fraction and localized to a specific radial range.

evidence.quantity: which empirical profile family best fits the projected photometry

value.conclusion: a Wilson (1975) model fits Omega Centauri's photometry better than a King (1962) model

evidence.limitations: This directly bears on approximation A in king-abel-profile.json (equating the 3D core radius to a projected King core radius): the literature says the projected profile family itself is better represented by a Wilson model for this cluster, so a King-only fit is known to be a worse choice of family, independent of which core radius is used. The specific fitted McLaughlin & van der Marel (2005) Wilson-model concentration and core radius for NGC 5139 were not retrieved from their Table 9 in this session (see mclaughlin-vandermarel-2005 source access note) -- this is a named gap, not an authored substitute value.

evidence.unit: dimensionless (d log I / d log r)
evidence.scope: Innermost several arcsec, HST ACS integrated light
evidence.limitations: Shows a shallow rising cusp rather than a flat King core at the very center; part of the still-debated intermediate-mass-black-hole literature for this cluster (not adjudicated here), and irrelevant at the parsec scales the bulk King-Abel profile in this ledger targets, but recorded because it shows the innermost profile shape is not simply flat.

evidence.scope: Whole cluster, Gaia EDR3 + HST + literature combination
evidence.limitations: Agrees with the ledger's existing 'distance' entry (5430 +/- 50 pc) to well within its stated uncertainty; recorded as a second, independently-titled peer-reviewed source rather than only the Baumgardt group's public website table, strengthening but not replacing the existing entry.

evidence.quantity: status note: position angle of the major axis on the sky

value.status: not solidly sourced in this session

evidence.limitations: Search-engine summaries in this session surfaced several candidate values (roughly 100, 103 and 108 degrees) attributed inconsistently to different studies (White & Shawl 1987, van de Ven et al. 2006, and later isodispersion-contour analyses), and one general note that White & Shawl (1987) and Chen & Chen (2010) disagree on position angle. None of these numbers were confirmed against a primary paper fetched directly in this session, so none is recorded as a value here. This is a genuine, reported gap: do not treat any of the numbers above as sourced. A future session should fetch White & Shawl (1987) and a recent isophotal/isodispersion fit directly (e.g. via the MUSE or HST proper-motion datasets) to pin this down before building an oriented oblate model.

evidence.quantity: status note: dedicated triaxial (three-axis) shape measurement
evidence.limitations: No paper performing a dedicated triaxial ellipsoid fit (e.g. from isophote twist, or a full triaxial Schwarzschild model) to Omega Centauri was located in this session. The evidence that exists and bears on the question is all indirect: the counter-rotating core (counter-rotating-core), the separate disk-like kinematic component (kinematic-disk-component), the tension between two independent axisymmetric inclination fits (inclination-van-de-ven-2006 vs inclination-haberle-2024), and the reported White & Shawl / Chen & Chen position-angle disagreement (position-angle-not-sourced). Together these say the cluster is not a perfectly simple single-axis oblate rotator, but none of them is itself a measured triaxial shape. This is recorded as a gap, not filled with an authored triaxiality value.
